title: Multi-Head Attention — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Parallel Attention Heads and Contextual Representation Learning · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Original questions without redundant Layer N prefixes, four balanced options per question, distinct diagrams, and beginner explanations with optional detail.
hero:
MULTI-HEAD ATTENTION · VISUAL OVERVIEW

One sentence. Multiple relationships at once.

Heads can find different clues in parallel. Their results are combined into a better contextual representation.

Swipe sideways to explore the diagram →

questions.stem: What is Multi-Head Attention in Transformer models, and how does using multiple Attention Heads allow a model to examine different relationships between words or tokens simultaneously instead of relying on a single Attention Mechanism?
options: Multi-head attention lets one head choose a single word and permanently discards all other relationships, so each token receives only one fixed source.
Multi-Head Attention runs several learned attention heads in parallel over token representations. Different heads can capture different relationships, and an output projection combines their results.
Multi-head attention creates new vocabulary words whenever the input contains unfamiliar spelling, rather than transforming the numerical features already provided.
Multi-head attention merges the entire sentence into one vector before calculating relevance, so separate token relationships cannot be examined by different heads.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Multi-Head Attention runs several learned attention heads in parallel over token representations. Different heads can capture different relationships, and an output projection combines their results. Imagine several editors reviewing a long newspaper article. One looks for names, another tracks dates, and another checks which event caused another. Multi-Head Attention gives a Transformer several learned attention mechanisms working on the same sequence. Each head can focus on different relationships and produce a contextual representation. The model then combines the head outputs so each token can use several kinds of context.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Each head learns its own query, key and value projections. It computes attention separately. The outputs are concatenated and projected, allowing diverse relationships, although some heads may be redundant.

questions.stem: Consider the sentence "The student opened the book because she wanted to study." How might different Attention Heads focus on different relationships, such as connecting "she" with "student," associating "book" with "opened," and understanding the purpose of "study"?
options: Every head is forced to make exactly the same attention connections, so the model cannot learn different patterns within the same sentence.
Only one attention head processes a sentence while the others remain inactive, meaning the architecture is effectively single-head during normal inference.
Every head is restricted to neighboring words, so pronouns cannot connect with distant nouns and action words cannot relate to later goals.
Different heads can attend to a pronoun's reference, a verb's object or more distant sentence context at once. These are learned tendencies, not fixed roles or a guarantee of unique head behavior.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Different heads can attend to a pronoun's reference, a verb's object or more distant sentence context at once. These are learned tendencies, not fixed roles or a guarantee of unique head behavior. Read “The student opened the book because she wanted to study.” One attention head may connect “she” with “student”. Another may link “opened” with “book”, while a third notices that “study” explains the purpose. These are possible learned patterns, not mandatory rules programmed into specific heads.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: These links illustrate possible attention patterns, not guaranteed roles for particular heads. Actual attention maps vary across head, layer, model, and input context.

questions.stem: How does information travel through a Multi-Head Attention layer, from receiving token representations and creating separate Query, Key, and Value vectors for each head to calculating attention independently, combining head outputs, and producing a final contextual representation?
options: Project inputs into Q, K and V for each head, calculate separate scaled attention outputs, concatenate the head results and apply the learned output projection WO.
The network first turns token IDs into final labels, then one head predicts the response while every other head copies exactly that same result.
Each head rearranges the original sentence into a new word order, after which the vocabulary layer generates attention scores without Query-Key comparisons.
The model adds head outputs together before creating Queries, Keys, or Values, placing the combination before the attention calculations that produce those outputs.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Project inputs into Q, K and V for each head, calculate separate scaled attention outputs, concatenate the head results and apply the learned output projection WO. Picture a wildlife-reporting system reading a description of animals moving near a river. It starts with token representations and creates Query, Key, and Value vectors. The projected features are split into separate attention heads. Each head compares Queries with Keys, normalizes scores, and combines Values into contextual features. The head outputs are joined, then a learned output projection mixes their information.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: The input is projected to per-head Q, K and V. Each head computes scaled dot-product attention. The outputs are concatenated and passed through the final W_O projection.

questions.stem: How does Multi-Head Attention divide the model's hidden dimensions across multiple heads, and how are scaled dot-product attention, Softmax, head concatenation, and the output projection matrix \(W_O\) mathematically combined to produce the final Attention output?
options: Each attention head always receives the full hidden width independently, and splitting features is unnecessary even in an implementation with fixed total projection width.
Heads divide sentence positions into separate groups and never share context across groups, rather than splitting projected feature dimensions to compute attention.
With dmodel=512 and eight equally sized heads, dhead is commonly 64. Each head applies QKᵀ/√dhead, a mask and softmax, then mixes V; concatenate heads and transform with WO.
The final output averages raw Query vectors without weighting Values, joining heads, or using the learned output projection matrix in the attention layer.
questions.explanation: Explanation: With dmodel=512 and eight equally sized heads, dhead is commonly 64. Each head applies QKᵀ/√dhead, a mask and softmax, then mixes V; concatenate heads and transform with WO. Imagine a Transformer with 512 hidden features and eight attention heads. A common design assigns 64 Query and Key features to each head, because 512 divided by eight is 64. Each head calculates scaled Query-Key scores, applies Softmax, and uses the weights to combine Values. The head outputs are concatenated and passed through WO, a learned matrix that mixes their information.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: For standard equal-size heads, d_head=d_model/h. Each head uses Softmax(QKᵀ/√d_head)V, and all head outputs are concatenated and multiplied by W_O.

questions.stem: How can Multi-Head Attention be implemented from scratch using Python and PyTorch, including reshaping Query, Key, and Value tensors, computing attention scores for multiple heads, applying causal masks, and verifying the output against PyTorch's built-in attention functions?
options: Create heads by stacking unchanged token IDs, then compare their labels after choosing the output token; this skips the actual learned attention calculation.
In PyTorch project and reshape Q/K/V to [batch,heads,tokens,dhead], apply scaled-dot-product attention and causal masks where needed, merge heads, then compare with a built-in reference.
Let PyTorch choose head dimensions automatically without arranging Query, Key, or Value tensors, and assume all input shapes are already valid.
Apply Softmax to raw token embeddings before making any head projections, so no Query-Key scores or causal masks can influence the attention result.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In PyTorch project and reshape Q/K/V to [batch,heads,tokens,dhead], apply scaled-dot-product attention and causal masks where needed, merge heads, then compare with a built-in reference. Suppose you are implementing a tiny next-token model for a command-line tool. In PyTorch, project the input into Q, K, and V tensors, then reshape them into attention heads. Calculate scores, apply a causal mask so future tokens are hidden, normalize with Softmax, and combine Values. Rejoin heads before the output projection.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: For [B,H,T,d] tensors, compute QKᵀ/√d, apply a causal mask before Softmax, multiply by V, then compare with F.scaled_dot_product_attention(...,is_causal=True).
questions.figure:
05 · PYTORCH

Split heads, mask the future, compare with built-in attention

Runnable PyTorch example
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
B, T, D, H = 2, 4, 8, 2
x = torch.randn(B, T, D)
W = torch.randn(D, 3 * D)
q, k, v = (x @ W).chunk(3, dim=-1)

def split(t):
    return t.reshape(B, T, H, D // H).transpose(1, 2)

q, k, v = map(split, (q, k, v))
scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / (D // H) ** 0.5
mask = torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool).tril()
manual = torch.softmax(scores.masked_fill(~mask, -torch.inf), -1) @ v
built_in = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)
torch.testing.assert_close(manual, built_in)
print(manual.shape)  # [2, 2, 4, 4]

Swipe sideways to explore the diagram →

The manual implementation and built-in scaled-dot-product attention should match within numerical tolerance.

questions.stem: Why do different Attention Heads sometimes learn specialized patterns while others become redundant, and how can head visualization, attention entropy, head pruning, and ablation experiments help researchers understand which heads contribute meaningfully to Transformer performance?
options: Inspect attention-weight maps and head entropy, but patterns alone do not prove importance. Ablation disables a head and measures the resulting task-quality change; pruning should preserve useful behavior.
Assign a permanent role to every attention head at initialization, guaranteeing no two heads can develop overlapping patterns through training.
Compare head weight sizes only, without measuring attention patterns or what happens to prediction accuracy when a head is removed.
Remove every head with focused attention because low entropy always means useless behavior, regardless of its contribution to the actual task.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Inspect attention-weight maps and head entropy, but patterns alone do not prove importance. Ablation disables a head and measures the resulting task-quality change; pruning should preserve useful behavior. Picture a research team examining a model that summarizes scientific articles. Some attention heads might follow section titles, while others repeatedly make similar connections. Researchers can visualize attention matrices and measure entropy to see whether a head's weights are focused or spread out. But a visual pattern does not prove usefulness. Ablation removes or disables a head and checks whether model performance changes.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Attention visualization and entropy describe where heads attend and how concentrated their weights are. Controlled ablation or pruning can reveal downstream impact, without assuming an attention map proves importance.

questions.stem: How do Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) differ in their Query-Key-Value organization, and how do FlashAttention, KV caching, and optimized attention kernels address memory bandwidth, computational complexity, and inference latency when scaling Large Language Models to long contexts?
options: MHA and MQA share all Query heads, while GQA stores more independent cached KV heads than MHA, reversing the expected memory arrangements.
MLA removes every stored context vector, so generation never needs old token information and can answer from the current token alone.
FlashAttention makes exact dense attention linear in sequence length, so adding more tokens no longer has quadratic computation costs in long contexts.

MQA shares KV heads across Queries, GQA shares by groups and MLA compresses cached states. FlashAttention tiles exact dense attention to reduce memory traffic without removing all pairwise computation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: MQA shares KV heads across Queries, GQA shares by groups and MLA compresses cached states. FlashAttention tiles exact dense attention to reduce memory traffic without removing all pairwise computation. Imagine a language model analyzing a long novel. Standard multi-head attention keeps separate Key and Value heads; that can require substantial KV-cache memory during generation. MQA shares a single KV head, and GQA shares groups. MLA can use compressed cached information. FlashAttention makes attention calculations more memory-efficient, but does not remove all pairwise compute from dense attention.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: MHA uses per-head K/V, MQA shares one K/V head, GQA has grouped K/V heads, and MLA caches latent features plus positional components. KV caching reuses prior states; FlashAttention uses IO-aware tiling but retains quadratic arithmetic for dense attention.
